narrative: Star Vetter automatically vets candidate eclipsing binary stars found in TESS satellite data. It starts with light curves from thousands of observed targets, applies statistical quality checks and cross-matches against six known variable-star catalogs to flag novel candidates, and then runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm that the signal comes from the target star itself rather than nearby contamination. So far, the pipeline has confirmed 110 candidates from 7,131 target observations covering 0.8% of the available sky. The vetting process is designed to be conservative: it uses a rule-based baseline with perfect recall (catches everything that passes) but low precision (many false positives), and supplements this with a machine-learning model trained on over 1,000 labeled examples. While Star Vetter's automated checks are thorough, individual candidates may still carry open caveats noted on their pages.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth's viewpoint, one star regularly passes in front of the other. Each eclipse causes a dip in the brightness of the system as seen in a light curve. These dips reveal the orbital period, the relative sizes of the stars, and how much light each star produces.

faqs.question: What does 'candidate' vs 'confirmed' mean on this site?
faqs.answer: A candidate is a light curve signal that passed statistical quality checks and was not found in six major known variable-star catalogs. A confirmed candidate has passed an additional automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the brightness change actually comes from the target star itself and not from a nearby star or instrumental artifact.

faqs.question: What is the machine-learning score and what does it do?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter uses a gradient-boosting machine-learning model, trained on 1,079 labeled examples, as a second opinion on which light curves look like real eclipsing binaries. It outperforms the rule-based baseline, but it is not used to decide which candidates get checked. All candidates that pass the statistical and novelty checks go to the pixel-level verification regardless of any score.

faqs.question: How is a candidate checked?
faqs.answer: Every candidate undergoes a fully automated pixel-level check. This check examines the spatial distribution of light in the image data to confirm that the eclipse signal originates from the target star itself, not from a nearby star or other source of contamination. Candidates that pass are marked as confirmed on this site.

faqs.question: What if the orbital period looks aliased?
faqs.answer: Aliasing can occur when the observation pattern creates ambiguity about the true period. Star Vetter checks for this by comparing the eclipse depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If the depths differ significantly, it suggests the period may be misidentified. This caveat is noted on the candidate's page if it applies.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate page includes links to the TESS light curve and the pixel-level check details, so you can examine the original data and the automated vetting results yourself.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on Star Vetter?
faqs.answer: Being listed here is the final step of this automated pipeline itself. Star Vetter does not perform spectroscopy, measure stellar masses, conduct follow-up observations, or submit candidates to official catalogs. What happens next - whether a candidate is observed by other astronomers, added to published surveys, or studied further - is outside the scope of this project.
